claims.text: As-processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
As-processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
As-processed HfZrTiTa0.53 exhibits 13.5% uniform strain under compression.
As-processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has limited tensile ductility.
HfZrTiTa0.53 possesses impact-triggered energy release that can be preserved by processing.
Cold deformation followed by short-time intermediate-temperature annealing can induce a bimodal grain structure in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Cold deformation creates a high density of dislocations in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Cold deformation refines the initial grain structure of HfZrTiTa0.53.
Controlled short-time annealing near 0.5 times the melting temperature produces selective recrystallization.
The annealing treatment causes grain coarsening only in selected regions.
Partially recrystallized softer regions restore tensile ductility.
A fine-grained matrix contributes to ductility in the proposed bimodal microstructure.
Coarser grains or retained nanoprecipitates preserve strength in the proposed bimodal microstructure.
Remaining fine-scale dislocation obstacles and precipitates maintain the alloy's strength after annealing.
Preserved dislocation obstacles and precipitates maintain impact-triggered energy release.
The treatment increases uniform tensile elongation by at least 50% relative to 13.5%, to approximately 20% or more.
The treated alloy retains yield strength within 10% of 786 MPa.
The treated alloy retains impact energy release comparable to that of the as-processed alloy.
The predicted benefit applies at room temperature under quasi-static loading below 10^-3 s^-1.
High temperatures or very high strain rates may negate the benefit through loss of the intended microstructural features, including grain growth.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% value is described as uniform strain under compression and also used as the baseline for uniform tensile elongation. Compression terminal or uniform strain is not interchangeable with uniform tensile elongation.
A 50% increase from 13.5% equals 20.25%, whereas the hypothesis and falsification rule use approximately 20% or merely exceeding approximately 20% as if it were the same threshold.

The scope is stated as quasi-static loading below 10^-3 s^-1 and the tests are described as being under matched conditions, but an impact penetration test necessarily uses a substantially different loading and strain-rate regime.
